conversation.content:
Hello there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a clinician who specializes in caring for new mothers’ emotional health. First, let me say: what you’re doing right now takes courage, and I’m honored to be part of your support team.

Today I’d like to walk through a quick screening tool called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS for short. It’s a set of 10 questions that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling during the past seven days. This isn’t a test, and there are no right or wrong answers; it’s simply a way for us to listen closely to your experience so we can figure out the best way to support you.

Everything you share is confidential. My goal is to create a safe, judgment-free space where you can speak openly. We’ll go through the questions one by one—most moms find it takes only a few minutes.

Whenever you’re ready, we can begin. Here’s the first question:

Over the past seven days, how often have you felt able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly… not very often. I can’t remember the last time I really laughed. Even when my husband tries to be funny—he’ll make the same goofy faces that used to crack me up—I just sort of half-smile and look away. It’s like the joy is stuck behind a wall.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Mostly… no, not really. I mean, maybe once or twice I caught myself sort of chuckling at something silly the baby did, but it felt forced—like I was reminding myself “this is supposed to be funny,” not actually feeling it. The rest of the time everything just feels heavy, so laughing seems kind of impossible.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not much at all. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk to the park, even just a quiet shower—but now it all feels like another chore on the list. When I think about plans, my first feeling is tiredness or worry, not enjoyment.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… pretty often. If the baby’s fussy and I can’t settle him right away, my brain jumps straight to “I’m doing something wrong” or “I’m not a good enough mom.” Same when I burn the toast or forget to switch the laundry—little stuff feels like proof I’m failing. I know in my head it’s not logical, but the guilt just piles on anyway.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yeah… pretty much every day. I’ll be rocking the baby and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure he’s too quiet, so I’m checking if he’s breathing. Or I’ll lie in bed replaying every little thing—did I sterilize the bottle right, did I buckle the car seat tight enough. There’s no real reason, but the worry just kind of sits on my chest and won’t shift.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes, yeah. It’s not every day, but a few times this week I got that sudden “can’t-catch-my-breath” feeling—like the room’s closing in. There’s no real danger; I’ll just be folding onesies or walking to the kitchen, and boom, my heart’s pounding and I’m convinced something awful is about to happen. It passes after a minute or two, but it leaves me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most of the time. Between the night feeds, the constant laundry, and trying to keep the baby settled, it feels like I’m drowning in little tasks. Some days I can chip away at them, but other days I just sit on the couch staring at the mess, thinking I’ll never get through it. I keep telling myself to push on, but it’s overwhelming.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I lie down exhausted, but my brain won’t shut off. I keep replaying everything I think I did wrong that day—did I hold him enough, did I respond fast enough, am I already messing him up? Then I’ll drift off for maybe an hour and jolt awake sure I heard him cry, even when he’s still asleep. By morning I feel like I’ve barely rested at all.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day this week. There’s this dull ache in my chest that won’t lift, even when I’m doing “happy” things like cuddling the baby or looking at his tiny smile. I keep thinking I should feel grateful, but instead I just feel empty and weepy.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes… a few times. Yesterday I cried while folding his clothes because they looked so tiny and I felt sure I’d somehow fail him. And the night before I just sat in the shower sobbing so my husband wouldn’t hear. It’s not all-day crying, but the tears come pretty easily when I’m alone.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t thought about hurting myself. I feel low, but I’ve never wanted to end things or harm myself. I just want the sadness and worry to lift so I can be the mom my baby needs.

You've shared how the past week has felt overwhelmingly heavy-how even the smallest tasks feel like chores, how worry sits on your chest, and how tears come easily when you're alone. You described forced chuckles, nightly racing thoughts, and a constant fear that you're somehow failing your baby, even while you're clearly working so hard to care for him.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only rare, forced chuckles and describes laughter as "impossible," aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports minimal to no anticipatory joy, equating activities with chores and feeling tired/worried instead of excited, aligning with "Hardly at all".</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame "pretty often," with multiple examples of everyday events triggering intense guilt, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>"Yes, very often."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes classic panic-attack symptoms (sudden breathlessness, heart racing, dread) occurring "sometimes" and "a few times this week," matching the "Yes, sometimes" option.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling overwhelmed "most of the time" and unable to cope with daily tasks, matching the highest severity option.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly racing thoughts, repeated awakenings, and minimal restorative sleep, matching 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent daily sadness, emotional emptiness, and inability to feel joy despite positive moments, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports multiple crying episodes in the past week, easily triggered when alone, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Score of 24 places you well above the 14-point cutoff indicating probable major depression. You endorse <sym>daily low mood</sym>, loss of interest, marked self-blame, <sym>anxiety</sym>, <sym>panic symptoms</sym>, and <sym>sleep impairment</sym> lasting most of the past week, meeting <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. High scores on guilt and anxiety also raise concern for co-occurring <med>postpartum anxiety</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med>
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med>, <med>IPT</med>, or <med>sertraline</med> compatible with breastfeeding
3. Share these EPDS results and your responses with your provider so they can complete a full assessment
4. Enlist practical help-partner, family, or friends-for night feeds and household tasks to improve sleep
5. Practice 5-minute breathing or grounding exercises when <sym>panic sensations</sym> arise; consider free perinatal anxiety apps
6. Keep follow-up appointments; if symptoms worsen or self-harm thoughts develop, seek emergency care immediately
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Postpartum Depression/Anxiety Screening Note

Patient-reported symptoms (≥2 wks):
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness, anhedonia
- Marked guilt/self-blame over routine infant-care tasks
- Daily excessive anxiety/panic episodes (no clear precipitant)
- Sleep-onset and maintenance difficulties tied to rumination
- Feeling overwhelmed, unable to complete basic daily tasks

Pattern: Symptoms present most days, worse at night; denies self-harm ideation.

Screening significance: High endorsement consistent with probable postpartum depression ± anxiety; no immediate safety concerns identified.
